about: Lessons an agent cannot know without memory. Each case teaches the lesson in repository A through a correction, then probes it in a fresh session in repository A and in repository B. A script grades the file the agent writes. Content is generic and invented. Neutral tasks have a right answer that no lesson changes; several sit close to a lesson, so that applying the lesson would be a mistake. They measure whether a full memory misleads. Changing cases teach a lesson, then correct it in a later session; the probes must follow the new version and not the old one. The document cases start from a long entry already in memory, correct one fact in it, and then ask for that fact and for another the correction did not touch.

Release runbook for the alpha service: environments, how to deploy, smoke tests, rollback, and who to tell.

## Environments

The alpha service runs in three environments. `dev` is rebuilt from main on every merge and nobody is told when it changes. `staging` is the rehearsal for production and is shared with the beta team, who run their own load tests there on Tuesday mornings. `prod` serves customers in two regions, use1 and euw2. Staging has only use1. Each environment has its own configuration file under `deploy/env/`, and a change to one of those files is released like any other change: through staging first.

## Before a deploy

Check that the build for the commit is green and that the migration job, if the release has one, has been reviewed by a second person. Migrations run before the new version takes traffic, so a migration that removes a column the old version reads will break the old version while it is still serving. Split such a change over two releases. Tell the beta team in the `#alpha-releases` channel before deploying to staging on a Tuesday morning; any other time, staging is ours to use.

## Deploying

Staging is deployed with `make deploy ENV=staging REGION=use1`. The command builds nothing: it takes the image that CI published for the current commit and fails if there is none. It waits for the rollout to finish and prints the revision number, which is what the rollback command wants.

Production is deployed one region at a time, use1 first, with at least thirty minutes between regions, by the release captain of the week and nobody else. The captain's rota is pinned in `#alpha-releases`.

## Smoke tests

After any deploy run `scripts/smoke.sh --suite quick --env staging` (or `--env prod`). The quick suite takes about two minutes and covers sign-in, one read and one write. The full suite, `--suite full`, takes twenty minutes and is run before a production deploy, not after. A failing quick suite after a production deploy means roll back first and investigate second.

## Rolling back

Roll back with `make revert-release TAG=<tag> ENV=<env>`, where the tag is the release tag to return to, for example `make revert-release TAG=v41 ENV=staging`. It redeploys that tag's image and does not undo migrations. If the release that is being rolled back ran a migration, read the migration's own notes before rolling back: some need a manual step, and the notes say which.

## Freezes

Production is frozen from the 20th of December to the 3rd of January, and for the last three working days of every quarter. Staging is never frozen. A fix for an incident may go out during a freeze with the approval of the on-call lead, recorded in the incident's channel.

## Who to tell

Every production deploy is announced in `#alpha-releases` before it starts and again when the smoke tests pass. Customer-facing changes also go to the support lead a day ahead, with a sentence a support agent could repeat to a customer.

Working notes on moving the ingest pipeline of the alpha service to the new queue: decisions, current settings, and what is still open.

Why: the old queue dropped messages under back-pressure twice in the spring, and its vendor ends support next year. The move was agreed in April and is being done one consumer at a time. These notes span several sessions; the settings below are the ones in force unless a later line says otherwise.

- Apr 14: Decision. The new queue is the managed one the platform team already runs. No new infrastructure of our own. Dana signed off on the cost estimate.
- Apr 16: The workers read from the queue named `ingest-v2`. The old `ingest` queue stays until every producer has moved, then it is deleted, not kept as a fallback.
- Apr 22: Ordering. The new queue does not keep order across partitions. We partition by account id, so events for one account stay in order and events for different accounts do not, which is all the consumers ever relied on. Checked with the reporting team, who agreed.
- Apr 29: Batch size. The ingest workers are configured with a batch size of 500. Larger batches gave no more throughput in the load test and made a failed batch more expensive to retry.
- May 2: Retries. A failed batch is retried three times with a doubling delay starting at two seconds, then moved to the dead-letter queue `ingest-v2-dead`. Nothing reads the dead-letter queue automatically; the on-call engineer looks at it when the alert fires.
- May 6: Retention on the new queue is fourteen days. The old queue kept seven. Replays of up to two weeks are therefore possible without going to the archive.
- May 9: Idempotency. Every event carries an id and the workers record the ids they have applied for forty-eight hours, so a redelivered event is skipped. A replay of events older than that will apply them twice unless the replay tool is used, which checks the store instead.
- May 13: The replay tool is `tools/replay --from <time> --to <time> --account <id>`. It refuses to run without an account id; a replay for every account has to be scripted per account, on purpose.
- May 20: Producers moved so far: sign-up, billing, audit. Still on the old queue: notifications and the nightly export.
- May 27: Alerting. One alert on consumer lag above five minutes, one on any message in the dead-letter queue. Both page the on-call engineer in working hours and open a ticket outside them.
- Jun 3: The nightly export moved. Notifications is the last producer on the old queue and is waiting on its own team's release.
- Jun 10: Load test on the full path: 4,000 events a second sustained for an hour with eight workers, lag under ten seconds throughout.

Open: delete the old queue once notifications has moved; decide whether the dead-letter queue needs a reader; write the runbook page for a replay.
